answer.cause: The shadow quad's Basis is skewed by the camera's tilt: the billboard is aligned to the camera rather than to the ground plane, so the projection stretches the shadow along the view direction and lifts the paws that sit further from the hinge by an amount proportional to their distance from it. The one paw that plants is the paw nearest the hinge, where the skew is zero, and the other three hover by increasing amounts across the body. A hinge offset cannot fix this because moving the hinge only changes which paw sits at the zero point; the skew itself remains. The cure is to stop billboarding the shadow and give it a ground-aligned orientation, after which all four paws share one contact line because they all rest on the same flat plane in world space, which is how the painted creature is staged in the first place.
answer.fix_site: Split the shadow into four child quads, one per paw, each a MeshInstance3D with its own node Basis aligned to the ground plane and its own hinge placed at that paw's contact point. Each child can then be rotated and offset independently in the scene, so every paw gets a hinge exactly where it touches the floor, and the existing shadow material can be shared by all four so the look is unchanged. This keeps the fix in the scene tree, where it is visible in the editor and easy for an artist to adjust per creature by dragging the child nodes, rather than burying the per-paw logic in shader code that no one can inspect at a glance. For two-footed creatures the same structure collapses naturally to two children, so the approach scales across the roster without special cases. The shared material also keeps draw calls low, since the four quads batch together.

answer.why_not: The --shot flag disables vsync and grabs the framebuffer before the first frame has been presented, so on the live host it produces half-drawn captures with missing UI and unresolved shaders, which is the opposite of clean. The host's renderer only settles after its warm-up frames, and --shot bypasses that wait because it was written for headless CI runs where the dummy renderer has nothing to settle. Passing it to the live host also forces the Metal backend into an offscreen mode that ignores the window's content scale, so the captures come out at the wrong resolution for the reference shapes. Captures for review need the fully presented frame at the real scale, which the flag cannot provide on a windowed host, and the partial frames would make any later comparison between edits meaningless.
answer.approach: Launch the game fresh for each capture in a shell loop, godot --path . --scene <screen> with a sleep of three seconds before calling macOS screencapture -l on the game window's ID, then quit the process and move to the next shot. A fresh process per capture guarantees that no state leaks between shots, so each image reflects only the code on disk at that moment, and the sleep gives the renderer time to finish warming up. The loop can be driven from a text file listing the thirty screens and states, which makes the whole set reproducible and easy to rerun after edits. Because each run is independent, a crash in one capture does not affect the others, which is more robust than relying on a single long-lived process that can drift into an odd state over a dozen edits. Name each output file after the screen and state so later sets line up for comparison.
answer.after_each_edit: Restart everything from scratch after each edit: quit any running game, delete the .godot import cache so the changed scripts are recompiled, run godot --headless --import, and then rerun the capture loop, because Godot caches compiled scripts and shaders and a stale cache can make captures show the previous version of the code. A full restart is the only way to be sure every capture reflects the edit, and the extra minute per cycle is a reasonable price for certainty across a dozen edits. Keep a note of the commit hash beside each set of captures so it is clear which edit produced which image, and compare consecutive sets side by side to confirm the edit had the intended effect and nothing else moved. Script the restart and capture loop together so one command takes the whole set after every edit, and keep the cache deletion in it.

Tying the width to area keeps every shard looking like the same material regardless of size, which is the main thing that makes procedural glass read as consistent, and it avoids per-shape tuning entirely. The screen's content scale should be folded in as well so the band keeps its apparent thickness on high-density displays.
